title: Psalm 58: There Is Surely a God Who Judges
summary: David confronts corrupt rulers who pervert justice, describes the wicked as liars from birth and deaf as a cobra, and asks God to break their teeth and make them vanish. The psalm ends with the righteous rejoicing at God's vengeance and all people confessing that there is a God who judges the earth.
story: Psalm 58 is the middle of three psalms (57 to 59) set to the tune “Do Not Destroy,” and it shifts the focus from David's personal enemies to injustice at the level of rulers and courts. It belongs to a group of psalms often called imprecatory, meaning psalms that call down curses or judgment on enemies (others include Psalms 35, 69, 109, and 137). Where Psalm 57 prayed for God's glory to cover the earth, Psalm 58 asks what that means when the people entrusted with justice are themselves the source of violence. Its answer is that the world is not finally ruled by the corrupt. Psalm 82, later in the Psalter, takes up the same theme of unjust judges answering to God.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David but gives no occasion, unlike its neighbors. Its concern with rulers who judge unjustly would fit many periods of Israel's history, from the abuses of Saul's court to the corrupt officials the prophets denounced in the eighth century BC (Isaiah 1:23; Amos 5:12; Micah 3:9-11). Israel's law required judges to be impartial and forbade bribes (Exodus 23:6-8; Deuteronomy 16:18-20), so a corrupt court was not only a social wrong but a breach of covenant.

The first line raises a translation problem. The Hebrew consonants are usually read as elem, silence, which gives an awkward sense (do you indeed speak righteousness in silence). Many translators change one vowel to read elim, mighty ones or gods, and the BSB renders it “rulers.” Some scholars think the psalm addresses human judges, called gods because they exercise God's authority to judge (compare Exodus 21:6 and Psalm 82:6, where the same kind of language appears). Others think the psalm addresses heavenly powers thought to stand behind earthly rulers, as some read Psalm 82. The second line, “O sons of men,” can be read either as addressing human beings or as saying the rulers judge human beings.
cultural:
Verses 4 and 5 draw on snake charming, a practice known across the ancient Near East and especially in Egypt. Charmers claimed the power to control serpents with chants and music, and Ecclesiastes 10:11 and Jeremiah 8:17 also mention it. The cobra here refuses to listen, stopping its ears, so the charmer's skill is useless. The image is of people so hardened that no word of warning or wisdom can reach them.

The curses in verses 6 to 9 use images from daily life. Water that runs off into dry ground and disappears, arrows with blunted tips, a slug that seems to melt as it leaves its slime trail, and a stillborn child are all pictures of something that comes to nothing. Verse 9 is one of the hardest lines in the Psalter to translate. It seems to picture a cooking fire of thorns, which burns hot and fast, and a storm that sweeps everything away before the pot has even warmed. The point is sudden, complete removal.
literary: The psalm moves in three parts. Verses 1 and 2 accuse the rulers directly with a question and its answer. Verses 3 to 5 describe the wicked in the third person, using the image of the deaf cobra. Verses 6 to 9 turn to God with a rapid series of curse-images. Verses 10 and 11 close with the response of the righteous and of humanity as a whole. The opening and closing frame the whole: the rulers are asked whether they judge rightly, and the last line answers that there is “a God who judges the earth.” The word for judging appears in both places. The poem's violence of language is deliberate; it matches the violence the rulers have done “on the earth” (verse 2) with God's judgment on the same earth.

outline.t: Liars from birth, deaf as a cobra
A prayer that God would break their power
The righteous rejoice: there is a God who judges

doctrines.note: The psalm's conclusion is that God is the judge of all the earth, and that injustice will not have the last word. Its hope for vengeance is placed in God's hands, not taken into the speaker's own.

Verse 3 says the wicked go astray from the womb. This is poetry about settled, habitual evil rather than a doctrinal statement, but it agrees with the Bible's wider teaching that wrongdoing runs deep in human nature (Psalm 51:5).

The psalm gives voice to people who suffer under corrupt power and see no human remedy. Its fierce prayer shows that anger at injustice can be brought honestly to God rather than suppressed or acted out.

words.note: Elem, silence. This is how the Hebrew of verse 1 reads as pointed, but the sense is difficult, and most modern translations follow a small change to elim, mighty ones or gods, rendered “rulers” in the BSB. The word choice matters because it decides whether the psalm addresses human judges, heavenly powers, or both.

Shaphat, to judge. In the Old Testament judging includes deciding cases, ruling, and putting things right, especially for the weak. The psalm opens by asking whether the rulers judge uprightly and closes by confessing that God judges the earth. The same verb frames the whole poem.

Naqam, vengeance. In the Old Testament vengeance is primarily God's prerogative (Deuteronomy 32:35), and it means the restoration of justice by a rightful authority, not private revenge. The righteous rejoice when they see justice done, not because they have taken it into their own hands.

christ: The New Testament agrees with this psalm that God will judge the earth, and it names the judge: God has appointed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by the man he has appointed, the risen Jesus (Acts 17:31; John 5:22). Paul tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35 (Romans 12:19), which is the same move this psalm makes when it hands vengeance to God. The martyrs in Revelation 6:10 still cry out to God about when he will judge and avenge their blood. Jesus also taught his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44). The Christian reader holds both: a real longing for God's justice and a real love for enemies, trusting that the cross shows God's judgment and mercy meeting.

hard.q: How can Scripture contain a prayer for God to break people's teeth and a picture of the righteous washing their feet in the blood of the wicked?
hard.a: Verse 10 says the righteous “will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked,” a battlefield image of total victory, and many readers find it shocking. Several responses are offered. First, the psalm is a prayer, not an action: the speaker gives his anger to God rather than taking revenge, and he asks God to act as judge. Second, the target is rulers who use violence against the helpless, and the prayer comes from the side of their victims. Third, the language is poetic hyperbole drawn from ancient war songs, and it expresses the hope that evil will be decisively ended. Some Christians have concluded that such prayers belong to an earlier stage of revelation and are fulfilled or surpassed by Jesus' command to love enemies. Others argue that they remain valid prayers for justice, especially for the oppressed, and that praying them is safer than suppressing the anger they express. Most agree that they must be read alongside the whole Bible's teaching on mercy and judgment.

questions: Where do you see injustice done by people in power? What would it look like to bring your anger about it to God honestly?
Verse 11 says, “There is surely a God who judges the earth.” Why might that truth be comforting rather than frightening?
How do you hold together a longing for God's justice and Jesus' call to love your enemies?
